a: After these events
t: A gap of nearly sixty years
p: Chapter 6 ended in 515 BC. Ezra's story begins under a later king, Artaxerxes, at least 57 years on.
b: The temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius I, 515 BC (6:15). "After these events" passes over the whole reign of Xerxes, the Ahasuerus of Esther, and lands in the reign of an Artaxerxes. Two Persian kings of that name fit the period: Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC) and Artaxerxes II (404–359 BC). If the "seventh year" of 7:7 belongs to the first, Ezra arrived in 458 BC, thirteen years before Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:1). If it belongs to the second, he arrived in 398 BC, long after Nehemiah. The book's order assumes the first. The arguments on both sides are set out on the chapter page.

a: there was Ezra son of Seraiah
t: Son of Seraiah, the last head priest
p: Seraiah was the head priest put to death by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC. "Son" here means descendant.
b: Seraiah was taken from the ruined temple and killed at Riblah (2 Kings 25:18–21). Ezra came at least 128 years later, so "son of" must mean "descendant of," as it often does in genealogies. Seraiah's son Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chronicles 6:14–15) and was the father of Jeshua, the high priest of the first return (Ezra 3:2). Ezra, then, came from the high priestly family but not from the line of the high priests of his own day, and he is never called high priest. His name is a short form of Azariah, "the LORD has helped," a name that occurs twice in his own family tree (7:1, 7:3).

a: son of Azariah, son of Meraioth
p: Beside the priestly line in 1 Chronicles 6, Ezra's family tree skips six names between Meraioth and Azariah.
b: 1 Chronicles 6:4–14 runs: Eleazar, Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki, Uzzi, Zerahiah, Meraioth, Amariah, Ahitub, Zadok, Ahimaaz, Azariah, Johanan, Azariah, Amariah, Ahitub, Zadok, Shallum, Hilkiah, Azariah, Seraiah. Ezra 7:1–5 climbs the same ladder in reverse, but jumps from Meraioth straight to the Azariah of 1 Chronicles 6:10: "Johanan fathered Azariah. It was this Azariah who was priest in the house Solomon built in Jerusalem" (1 Chronicles 6:10). Missing are Johanan, Azariah, Ahimaaz, Zadok (David's priest), Ahitub and Amariah. A copyist could have produced this by an eye-skip between two similar names ending in -yah: after writing "son of Azariah," the eye fell on the earlier "son of Amariah" and went on from there with "son of Meraioth." Or the writer shortened the line on purpose, as genealogies often do, keeping sixteen ancestors from Aaron to Seraiah. Every name Ezra does give has the same Hebrew form as in Chronicles.

a: son of Aaron the head priest
p: The list ties Ezra to Aaron through Eleazar, Phinehas and Zadok, the line Ezekiel said alone could serve at the altar.
b: After the exile a priest had to prove his descent; those who could not were barred from the priesthood (2:61–63). Ezra's line runs through Phinehas, promised "a covenant of priesthood for all time" (Numbers 25:13), and through Zadok, whose sons Ezekiel named as the only priests allowed to approach the altar (Ezekiel 44:15). By giving the family tree before he calls Ezra a scribe, the book makes his authority priestly first. The two tasks meet in him: priests were charged to teach Israel the LORD's rules (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10), and Ezra the priest is also Ezra the teacher of the law.

a: He was a scribe, an expert in Moses' law
p: Sofer meant a trained writer and royal official. In Ezra it begins to mean a scholar of God's law.
b: In the courts of Judah a sofer was a royal secretary (2 Kings 22:3). The Persian letter gives Ezra a title, "scribe of the law of the God of the heavens" (7:12, 7:21), which Hans Heinrich Schaeder read as an office: the king's secretary for Jewish religious affairs. Others take it as the Jewish community's description of Ezra, written into the letter. Either way, the narrator explains the word in a new direction: a scribe is one who searches out, keeps and teaches the law (7:10). That road leads to the scribes of the Gospels and to the rabbis. The adjective mahir, "quick, practiced," stands with "scribe" in Psalm 45:1 and describes a skilled worker in Proverbs 22:29.

a: Because the LORD his God's hand was on him
p: A refrain of Ezra's story: six times the success of a human plan is credited to God's hand.
b: The phrase recurs at 7:6, 7:9, 7:28, 8:18, 8:22 and 8:31, and Nehemiah uses it of his own mission (Nehemiah 2:8; Nehemiah 2:18). It explains how a Persian king came to favor a Jewish priest without any miracle: the king grants Ezra's requests because God is behind them. The same God stirred Cyrus's spirit (1:1) and turned the heart of the Assyrian king toward his people (6:22). The book's view of the empire is here in small: foreign kings act freely, yet they serve God's purposes.

a: the temple servants
p: Hebrew netinim means "the given ones," workers given to serve the temple, possibly of foreign descent.
b: On the name, the foreign-sounding family names and the tradition that they came from the Gibeonites, see 2:43. The name, from natan, "give," also echoes the Levites who were "given" to Aaron (Numbers 8:19). What this part adds is a tension. The rabbis held the temple servants to be of Gibeonite descent and barred marriage with them (Bavli Yevamot 78b–79a). Yet Ezra brings 220 more of them to Jerusalem (8:20) to serve in the temple, in the same months in which chapter 9 condemns marriage with outsiders. The book does not comment on it.

a: in the fifth month
p: Leaving in the first month (March–April) and arriving in the fifth (July–August), the caravan traveled about four months.
b: If the king is Artaxerxes I, Ezra left in early April and arrived in early August of 458 BC. The road from Babylon to Jerusalem ran up the Euphrates and down through Syria, about 900 miles; for a large company with children and treasure that meant some 100 days on the march (see 8:31). Setting out in the first month, the month of Passover, recalls the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 12:2). Isaiah had pictured the return from Babylon as a second exodus (Isaiah 48:20; Isaiah 52:11–12), and Ezra's account carries that shape.

a: searching out
p: The verb is darash, "seek." Seeking God now includes searching his written word, the root of the later word midrash.
b: Earlier books use darash for seeking God himself (Deuteronomy 4:29; 1 Chronicles 16:11) or for consulting a prophet. Here Ezra seeks "the LORD's law," and his seeking means study. From this root came midrash, the Jewish name for searching out the meaning of Scripture, and beit midrash, a house of study. The verse's order caught readers' attention: Ezra studies, then does, then teaches. Jewish teachers drew the lesson that a teacher must live what he teaches; compare the saying in Mishnah Avot 1:17 that study is not the main thing, but doing. "Rules and rulings" (choq u-mishpat) is Deuteronomy's pair for the whole of the law (Deuteronomy 4:1).

a: a copy of the document
t: Persian words for a Persian letter
p: Both nouns are Persian loanwords. The writer marks what follows as an official document.
b: Parshegen, "copy," and nishtevan, "letter, document," come from Persian and appear in the Bible only in Ezra (4:7, 4:11, 4:18, 4:23, 5:5, 5:6); a form of the first also occurs in Esther 3:14 and Esther 4:8. The introduction is in Hebrew. With the next verse the language switches to Aramaic, the official language of the Persian Empire, and stays there through 7:26. Like the letters in 4:8–6:18, this one is presented as a copy from the royal file.

a: Artaxerxes, king of kings
p: From here to 7:26 the text is in Aramaic. "King of kings" is the Persian emperors' own title.
b: Old Persian xšāyaθiya xšāyaθiyānām, "king of kings," opens the royal inscriptions at Behistun and Persepolis. The Bible gives the title to Nebuchadnezzar (Ezekiel 26:7; Daniel 2:37) and, transformed, to God and Christ (1 Timothy 6:15; Revelation 19:16). The letter follows the pattern of Aramaic letters of the Persian period: sender, addressee, greeting, then "and now" to begin the business (compare 4:11, 4:17). Its Persian loanwords, such as asparna, "exactly" (7:17, 7:21, 7:26), and gizbar, "treasurer" (7:21), are what one would expect of a real chancery letter. Whether it was drafted at court, by Jewish officials for the king's seal, or later, is discussed on the chapter page.

a: full greeting
t: A puzzling word in the greeting
p: The Aramaic gemir means "complete." Where it belongs in the sentence is unclear.
b: The address ends with two words, gemir u-khe'enet. The second is the usual "and now" that turns to business (4:10–11, 4:17). The first means "complete, perfect." Three readings are offered. (1) It is a shortened greeting, "peace in full" (KJV "perfect peace"), perhaps because a copyist dropped the word shelam, "peace." The Plain takes this view. (2) It belongs to Ezra's title: "the perfect scribe of the law," that is, fully learned. (3) It is an archivist's "and so on," marking a greeting left out of the copy. The Greek of 2 Esdras (Rahlfs) reads tetelestai ho logos kai hē apokrisis, "the word and the answer are complete," taking both words as a statement.

a: the God of the heavens
p: Jews and Persians of the period both used this title for Israel's God.
b: On the title in Cyrus's edict, see 1:2. Here it is the king's own phrase, and the letter uses it four times (7:12, 7:21, 7:23 twice), always for the God whose law Ezra carries. To a Persian it could suggest a high, universal god like Ahuramazda; to a Jew it said that the LORD rules the whole sky. Nehemiah uses it in prayer (Nehemiah 1:4–5), so it was not only a diplomatic name.

a: whoever of the people of Israel
p: As under Cyrus, no one is forced to go. The king's decree permits; it does not command.
b: The same was true in 1:3–6. Many Jews had done well in Babylonia, and Ezra's company of about 1,500 men (8:1–14) was small beside the community that stayed. The Babylonian Talmud later said that Ezra did not leave until he had made Babylon's families "like fine flour," sifted for pure descent (Bavli Kiddushin 69b). That reading ties this journey to the concern with lineage that runs through chapters 8–10.

a: his seven counselors
p: Persian kings were advised by a council of seven nobles, known also from Esther and from Greek writers.
b: Esther 1:14 names seven officials of Persia and Media "who saw the king's face," that is, had direct access to him. The Greek historian Herodotus tells of seven noble conspirators who put Darius I on the throne and whose families kept the right to enter the king's presence (Histories 3.84). Ezra's mission carries the authority of the king and his inner council together.

a: to inspect
p: The verb bqr means to examine or oversee. What exactly Ezra was sent to do is debated.
b: Was Ezra an inspector reporting to the king, a judge, a teacher, or the leader of a religious reform? Richard Steiner compared the Aramaic verb with the Greek episkopos, the "overseer" Athens sent to its subject cities, and with the mebaqqer, the "overseer" of the Dead Sea Scrolls community. On this reading Ezra was a royal inspector with legal powers. Others stress the religious frame: he inspects "by the law of your God," so the standard is the Torah, and his tools are teaching and appointing judges (7:25). The same verb is used for searching the royal archives (4:15, 4:19, 6:1). The letter mixes both roles, which may be the point: the empire gave local law the backing of royal law (7:26).

a: by the law of your God that is in your hand
p: The Torah as we have it, part of it, or a priestly law book? The text does not say, and readers have long disagreed.
b: The whole Torah. Jewish and Christian tradition, and many modern scholars, take it as the five books of Moses. When Ezra reads it aloud (Nehemiah 8), it includes the Feast of Booths that Leviticus 23:39–43 commands, and Ezra 9:11–12 draws on both Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Some details in Nehemiah 8:15 match no surviving passage exactly, which shows how freely the law was applied. Part of it. Since Wellhausen, some critics have thought Ezra brought the Priestly laws, newly finished in Babylon; others have argued for Deuteronomy. A law the empire recognized. Peter Frei proposed that Persia authorized local laws as royal law, so that Ezra's law became binding as "the king's law" (7:26); contributors to James Watts's Persia and Torah doubt such a policy existed. "In your hand" can mean a scroll he carried or a law in his keeping.

a: who makes his home in Jerusalem
p: The letter speaks the language of the empire: each god has a city and a house, and the king honors them.
b: The Cyrus Cylinder boasts that Cyrus returned the gods of many cities to their shrines. The Egyptian official Udjahorresnet records that Darius I sent him home to restore the House of Life, the temple school, at Sais. Ezra's letter fits that policy: a Persian king, anxious for his realm (7:23), funds a god in his own house. The Jewish narrator sees more: the God of Israel is "the God of the heavens" (7:12), whom the king serves without fully knowing him (7:27).

a: you will be sure to buy
p: The Persian loanword asparna, "exactly, diligently," runs through the royal orders in Ezra.
b: The word appears in 5:8, 6:8, 6:12, 6:13, 7:17, 7:21 and 7:26. It marks a royal command to be carried out in full and without delay. The Plain varies the English ("be sure to," "to the letter," "strictly") to suit each sentence.

a: every treasurer in Beyond the River
p: Persian treasurers (gizzabrayya, from Persian ganzabara) managed royal stores across the empire.
b: On the title and the Persepolis treasury tablets, see 1:8, where Mithredath bears it. Beyond the River (Akkadian Ebir-nari) was the satrapy west of the Euphrates, taking in Syria, Phoenicia, Samaria and Judah. The letter lets Ezra draw on its treasurers up to a ceiling (7:22), like the earlier order to pay the temple's costs from the province's tribute (6:8–9).

a: as much as 100 talents of silver
t: How much is a hundred talents?
p: About three tons of silver, a large sum, though the other limits are modest.
b: A talent weighed roughly 30 kilograms (66 pounds), so 100 talents is around 3,000 kilograms of silver. Herodotus says the whole fifth satrapy, which included Beyond the River and Cyprus, paid the king 350 talents a year (Histories 3.91). A kor of wheat was perhaps 200 to 250 liters, so 100 kors is around 600 bushels; a bath was about 22 liters, so 100 baths of wine or oil is close to 600 gallons. Salt, needed with every grain offering (Leviticus 2:13), is unlimited. Some scholars think the silver figure is inflated; others note that it is a ceiling, not a gift.

a: Why let anger come on the kingdom of the king and his sons?
p: Persian kings feared the anger of foreign gods. In 458 BC there was a practical worry too: Egypt was in revolt.
b: Darius had asked the Jews to pray for the life of the king and his sons (6:10). Artaxerxes I came to the throne in 465 BC after his father Xerxes was murdered, and from about 460 to 454 BC Egypt rebelled with Athenian help. A king facing that war had reasons to secure the loyalty of a province on the road to Egypt, and the favor of its god. On the later date (398 BC), Egypt had again broken away (from 404 BC), so the setting suits either king, as advocates of each date point out.

a: tribute, tax or duty
p: The three taxes are the ones named in the complaint of 4:13. Every rank of temple worker is exempted.
b: Mindah, belo and halakh were probably the regular tribute, a tax in kind or a poll tax, and a toll or land tax; the exact sense of each is uncertain. Exempting the clergy of a favored temple was a known royal gift in the ancient world. A Greek inscription has Darius I rebuking his official Gadatas for taxing the sacred gardeners of Apollo, though its authenticity is disputed. The exemption made temple service attractive, which may be why the letter names every rank, down to the temple servants.

a: Anyone who does not know them, you are to teach
p: Ezra's courts were for "all who know your God's laws," that is, the Jews of the province, with teaching for the rest.
b: The letter does not give Ezra power over every resident of Beyond the River. His judges serve those who already know the laws of his God, the Jewish communities of the satrapy, and the verb "you are to teach" is plural, so the task belongs to Ezra and his judges together. Those who do not know the laws may be Jews who had drifted from them, or outsiders who chose to learn them. Judges joined with teaching echoes Moses' appointment of judges (Exodus 18:21–26; Deuteronomy 1:15–17) and Jehoshaphat's reform (2 Chronicles 19:5–10).

a: your God's law and the king's law
p: The letter sets God's law beside the king's law and backs both with the empire's penalties.
b: Readers weigh this differently. For many it shows the Torah gaining the force of imperial law in Judah, so that Persian courts could enforce it. Lisbeth Fried argues that "the king's law" is simply Persian law and that Ezra's job was imperial: setting up courts loyal to the crown. Others hear a Jewish voice in the letter (the sacrifices, the singers, "the God of the heavens") and suspect Jewish drafters wrote the pairing, so that obedience to God and loyalty to the king would look like one thing. Either way, the community that rebuilt Jerusalem lived under two authorities, a tension later Jews felt again under Rome (Mark 12:17).

a: or being rooted out
p: The Aramaic sheroshi comes from "root." Most take it as banishment; some as corporal punishment.
b: The written text and the reading in the margin spell the word slightly differently, and its sense is not certain. "Rooting out" suits banishment from the community, the penalty Ezra later threatens in 10:8. Others connect it with a Persian word for punishment, which would mean flogging. The other penalties are clear: death, a fine on property (literally "a penalty on goods") and "bonds," imprisonment.

a: Blessed is the LORD, God of our ancestors!
p: The language returns to Hebrew and the voice to "I." Ezra's own account runs to 9:15.
b: Scholars call 7:27–9:15 the Ezra Memoir. Its first-person voice resembles Nehemiah's memoir (Nehemiah 1–7; Nehemiah 12–13). Chapter 10 tells the end of the story in the third person, and Nehemiah 8 tells Ezra's reading of the law the same way. Many think the book's editor reworked a longer memoir, moving or retelling parts of it; Charles Torrey thought the memoir was the editor's own invention in Ezra's name. Most commentators today take the first-person sections as based on Ezra's own record. Fittingly, the memoir opens with praise before it gives any plans.

a: to make the LORD's house in Jerusalem beautiful
p: The verb pa'ar, "beautify, glorify," is the one Isaiah uses for God's future splendor on his temple.
b: Isaiah 60:7 promises, "I will make my splendid house more splendid still," and Isaiah 60:13 speaks of the cedar and cypress of Lebanon coming "to bring beauty to the site of my holy place." Ezra may be hinting that Persian gifts are the start of the promise that the wealth of the nations would come to Zion (Isaiah 60:5–13; Haggai 2:7–9). The temple had stood finished for decades. What it lacked was splendor.

a: To me he has stretched out loyal love
p: Hesed, God's covenant loyalty, reaches Ezra through a foreign court. The phrase returns in 9:9.
b: "Stretch out hesed" is the same expression Ezra uses in his prayer: God "has stretched out loyal love to us" before the kings of Persia (9:9). The word normally describes faithfulness within a covenant (Exodus 34:6; Deuteronomy 7:9). Ezra sees the Persian king's favor as one form that covenant loyalty takes: God keeps his promises to Israel through the empire's goodwill.

a: Here are the heads of the ancestral families
p: Twelve lay families, 1,496 men, plus two priestly houses, a descendant of David, and later Levites.
b: All twelve lay family names occur in the list of the first return (2:3–15), so these men were joining relatives already settled in Judah. Twelve families may be meant to stand for the twelve tribes, as the offerings of 8:35 do. The men total 1,496, plus 38 Levites and 220 temple servants (8:18–20). With women and children the company may have numbered 5,000 or more, still a small group beside the 42,360 of the first return (2:64). 1 Esdras 8:28–40 gives the same list with some different names and numbers.

a: Of the descendants of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the descendants of Ithamar, Daniel.
p: Both priestly houses descended from Aaron are present: Eleazar's (through Phinehas) and Ithamar's.
b: 1 Chronicles 24:3–4 divides the priests into Eleazar's line, which included Zadok, and Ithamar's line. Gershom and Daniel are heads of priestly houses, not single men traveling alone. This Daniel is not the prophet of the book of Daniel, though a priest named Daniel also seals the covenant in Nehemiah 10:6. Ezra's own line ran through Phinehas (7:5).

a: Of the descendants of David, Hattush,
t: A son of David in the caravan
p: Hattush was a descendant of Zerubbabel. The royal line travels with Ezra but holds no office.
b: 1 Chronicles 3:22 lists him among Zerubbabel's descendants: "The sons of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. The sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat, six" (1 Chronicles 3:22). In Ezra 7–10 a son of David is one traveler among many, and leadership belongs to the priest and scribe. Some readers see here a quiet fading of hope in the house of David. Others note that the family's survival kept the promise alive (2 Samuel 7:16; Zechariah 12:7–10), as the Gospel genealogies later stress (Matthew 1:12–13).

a: of the descendants of Shecaniah
p: The Hebrew begins 8:3 with "of the descendants of Shecaniah," which belongs with Hattush in 8:2.
b: Every other entry has a clan, a leader and a number. Read strictly by its verse division, the Masoretic text makes Shecaniah a clan with no leader and no number. 1 Chronicles 3:22 makes Hattush a grandson of Shecaniah, and 1 Esdras 8:29 (the same number in the KJV and in Rahlfs) reads "Hattush, the son of Shecaniah." So the phrase most likely completes 8:2: Hattush, of Shecaniah's family. The Plain keeps the Hebrew verse division but runs the sentence across it.

a: the last of them
p: Hebrew acharonim may mean the last members of the clan to return, or the younger branch of it.
b: Adonikam's family had already sent 666 men with the first return (2:13). Many take "the last" to mean the rest of the clan, who now came to complete the family's return. Others read it as "the younger ones," junior branches of the house. Only here does the list name three leaders instead of one, so the phrase probably marks a group rather than a single head.

a: the river that runs to Ahava
p: Ahava is unknown outside Ezra. The "river" was probably one of Babylonia's many irrigation canals.
b: Babylonia was crossed by canals, and the exiles had lived beside them from the start: Ezekiel saw his visions by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 1:1), and Psalm 137:1 remembers weeping by the rivers of Babylon. Business records of the Murashu firm at Nippur (455–403 BC) show men with Hebrew names among the farmers and tenants of a region laced with canals. Ahava may name both a town and its canal (8:21, 8:31). A three-day camp let the caravan gather and take stock before setting out.

a: not one descendant of Levi could I find there
p: Levites were scarce after the exile, and Ezra's caravan has none at first.
b: On the small number of Levites in the first return and the reasons usually given for it, see 2:36. Here the shortage is total. Life in Babylonia may have offered Levites more than hard work at a poor temple. Ezra's refusal to set out without them shows how much he wanted the temple staffed as the law of Moses and David's arrangements required (1 Chronicles 23:1–32).

a: who were teachers
p: The Hebrew calls Joiarib and Elnathan mevinim, "men who understand" or "who make others understand."
b: The participle can describe insight or the act of explaining. In Nehemiah 8:7–9 the same word names the Levites who helped the people understand the law as Ezra read it, and in 1 Chronicles 25:8 it describes skilled musicians teaching pupils. The Greek of 2 Esdras 8:16 has synientas, "men of understanding." The Plain's "teachers" takes the sense of Nehemiah 8, which fits Ezra's mission to teach the law (7:10, 7:25), but it is an interpretation: the men may only have been wise.

a: the head man at the place called Casiphia
p: Casiphia is unknown. Calling it "the place" may hint that it was a Jewish religious center.
b: The text twice says "the place Casiphia," an odd phrase. Deuteronomy uses "the place" for the sanctuary the LORD chooses (Deuteronomy 12:5), and some scholars suggest Casiphia had a Jewish shrine or school, perhaps like the Jewish temple at Elephantine in Egypt. That would explain why Levites and temple servants were found there under a leader, Iddo, and why Ezra sent teachers (8:16) to ask for them. The idea is attractive but unproved. The name may come from kesef, "silver."

a: the temple servants at the place Casiphia
t: A line the scribes found hard
p: The verse has two Ketiv-Qere pairs, and the vowels of "his brother" are also in doubt.
b: The written text has "I brought them out" and "those who are given," where the margin reads "I commanded them" and "the temple servants." The Masoretic vowels then make Iddo "his brother," singular, beside the plural "temple servants." The Plain reads the same letters as "his brothers," with the Greek versions (see the variant on "Iddo and his kinsmen"). Another option keeps the Masoretic vowels and has Ezra address Iddo and also "his brother," an unnamed second leader. The scribes, too, found the line difficult.

a: a man of good sense
t: A man of insight, or a name?
p: Ish sekhel means "a man of insight." Some take it as a proper name, Ish-sechel.
b: The Hebrew reads "they brought us a man of insight from the sons of Mahli... and Sherebiah," and the "and" leaves it unclear whether the man of insight is Sherebiah or someone else. Most translations make Sherebiah the man of insight, as the Plain does. Sherebiah became an important Levite: he helped explain the law at Ezra's reading (Nehemiah 8:7) and led prayer and praise (Nehemiah 9:4–5; Nehemiah 12:24). He is also one of the guardians of the gifts (8:24).

a: I called for a fast
p: Fasting was a way to humble oneself before God and ask for help in danger.
b: "Humble ourselves" is the verb used for the fast of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Fasting before a dangerous venture appears again with Jehoshaphat facing invasion (2 Chronicles 20:3) and Esther before she went to the king (Esther 4:16). Ezra fasts to seek "a straight road," the phrase of Psalm 107:7, where God leads wanderers on a straight road to a city where they can live. Isaiah's call to make a straight highway for God through the desert (Isaiah 40:3) may lie in the background, since the return from Babylon was pictured as a new exodus.

a: I was ashamed to ask the king
t: Ezra and Nehemiah on the road
p: Ezra refused an armed escort because of what he had told the king. Nehemiah later accepted one.
b: Nehemiah traveled with army officers and horsemen sent by the king (Nehemiah 2:9). Readers compare the two. Some praise Ezra's faith and find Nehemiah's escort less trusting. Others say both were right: Ezra had made a public claim about God's protection and could not undercut it, while Nehemiah went as governor, and an escort suited his rank. A third view notes that Ezra carried a fortune (8:26–27) and admits his fear; his fast is honest, not boastful. What he had told the king echoes the prophet Azariah's words to Asa (2 Chronicles 15:2) and Hanani's (2 Chronicles 16:9).

a: he was moved by our pleading
t: God let himself be won over
p: The verb 'atar in this form means God allowed himself to be moved by prayer, as with David and Manasseh.
b: The same verb ends the plague after David's offering (2 Samuel 24:25), answers Isaac's prayer for Rebekah (Genesis 25:21) and describes God's response to Manasseh's prayer in exile (2 Chronicles 33:13). It is a bold way of speaking: God is moved. Ezra records the answer before he tells the journey, and the safe arrival in 8:31 is the proof.

a: and with them Sherebiah, Hashabiah and ten of their brothers
p: Sherebiah and Hashabiah were Levites (8:18–19), so the guard was probably twelve priests and twelve Levites.
b: The Hebrew says "twelve of the chief priests, to Sherebiah, Hashabiah." Read literally, it seems to make the two Levites priests. Most interpreters take the little word le- as "together with," or assume an "and" dropped out. The pairing of priests and Levites fits 8:30 and 8:33, where both receive and hand over the gifts, and Numbers 4, where Levites carry the holy things under priestly charge.

a: 650 talents of silver
p: About 20 tons of silver and 3 tons of gold, a sum many scholars think too large to be literal.
b: At about 30 kilograms (66 pounds) a talent, the silver weighs some 19,500 kilograms and the gold some 3,000. The silver alone is nearly two years of the satrapy's tribute (Herodotus 3.91; see the note at 7:22), and gold was worth about thirteen times as much as silver. Some defend the figures as possible for gifts from the king, his court and a wealthy community abroad. Others suspect inflation for effect, or a confusion of units (minas, a sixtieth of a talent, for talents). The Hebrew of the silver vessels is also odd, "silver vessels, a hundred, by talents," as if a number had dropped out. The point is clear in any case: an enormous treasure was handed to holy men and carried across the desert without loss.

a: 1,000 darics
p: The daric was the Persian gold coin, named after Darius I and first struck around 515 BC.
b: Hebrew adarkonim is a loan from the Persian coin's name. A daric weighed about 8.4 grams, just over a quarter ounce, so 1,000 darics is about 8.4 kilograms (18.5 pounds) of gold. The same word appears in David's day in 1 Chronicles 29:7, where the Chronicler expresses the old gifts in the money of his own time. Here, in Ezra's memoir, it is the coin he would have handled.

a: You belong to the LORD as holy men, and the vessels are holy things too
p: Only consecrated people could carry consecrated things. Ezra applies the rule of the wilderness march.
b: In the wilderness the priests covered the holy furniture and the Kohathite Levites carried it: "They must not touch the holy things. If they do, they will die" (Numbers 4:15). Ezra's caravan follows that order on a new journey. Holy men guard holy vessels, and the gifts are weighed out at the start (8:26) and weighed in again at the temple (8:33–34). The care with numbers is itself a kind of holiness: nothing given to God goes missing.

a: on the twelfth of the first month
p: The caravan left the canal on the 12th of the first month, two days before Passover, and reached Jerusalem on the 1st of the fifth.
b: Ezra left Babylon on the 1st of the first month (7:9), camped by the Ahava, waited for Levites and fasted, then set out on the 12th. Passover fell on the 14th (Exodus 12:6), so it must have come while they were on the road; the memoir does not say how they kept it. The march took about 108 days. The terse "He saved us" covers months of danger from raiders on the desert routes.

a: For all Israel there were 12 bulls, 96 rams
p: The numbers are built on twelve: an offering for the whole twelve-tribe people, though few tribes were present.
b: Twelve bulls and twelve goats, and 96 rams (eight times twelve), echo the twelve goats offered for Israel's twelve tribes at the temple's dedication (6:17). Seventy-seven lambs breaks the pattern. 1 Esdras has 72, six times twelve, which may be the older figure (see the variant). The returned exiles saw themselves as all Israel, not just Judah and Benjamin, and Elijah's altar of twelve stones made the same claim long before (1 Kings 18:31).

a: the people of the exile, presented
p: In Ezra–Nehemiah the golah, "the exile," is the name of the true community, even after it has come home.
b: The verse piles up the phrase: "those who came from the captivity, the sons of the exile." Ezra–Nehemiah uses "the exile" or "the people of the exile" for the returned community (4:1; 6:19–21; 9:4; 10:7–8; 10:16). The identity is striking: decades after the return, belonging is defined by having gone through exile. Those who had stayed in the land are, by contrast, "the people of the land" (4:4) or "the peoples of the lands" (9:1). Some scholars read this as the outlook of a group that needed to justify its claim to land and temple; others as the mark of a community renewed by judgment and grace (9:8; Jeremiah 24:4–7).

a: the royal satraps
p: A satrap ruled one of the empire's great regions; under him, governors ran provinces such as Judah.
b: Hebrew achashdarpenim renders Old Persian xšaçapāvan, "protector of the realm." Beyond the River had one satrap and several provincial governors (pachot), among them the governors of Samaria and Judah. (Tattenai in 5:3 held a higher office, over the whole of Beyond the River.) Ezra's papers went up the chain of command, and the officials "lifted up" the people and the temple, that is, supported them. The journey ends with the empire on Ezra's side, so the crisis of chapter 9 comes from within the community, not from outside.

a: Once these things were done
p: Ezra arrived in the fifth month; the assembly over the marriages met in the ninth (10:9). Something filled the gap.
b: "These things" may be the handing over of the gifts and the offerings of 8:33–36. Three answers are given for what came between. (1) Charles Torrey, Wilhelm Rudolph, Jacob Myers and H. G. M. Williamson think Ezra's public reading of the law in the seventh month (Nehemiah 8) originally stood here, between Ezra 8 and 9; the officials' report would then follow the people's hearing of the law, which explains their sudden concern about the marriages. (2) 1 Esdras shows that the reading was once joined to Ezra's story, but it places it after Ezra 10, after the divorces (1 Esdras 9:37–55), which supports a different order. (3) Derek Kidner, Charles Fensham and Tamara Eskenazi keep the canonical order and read it as deliberate: the report came soon after Ezra's arrival, and the book saves the reading of the law for the climax in Nehemiah 8.

a: the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians
t: An old list for new neighbors
p: The officials combine the Canaanite nations of Deuteronomy 7 with the peoples Deuteronomy 23 keeps out of the assembly.
b: Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites and Amorites come from the list of Canaan's nations in Deuteronomy 7:1 (compare Exodus 34:11). Ammonites and Moabites come from Deuteronomy 23:3, and Egyptians from Deuteronomy 23:7, though that law actually lets Egyptians enter after three generations. Most of these nations had long disappeared by Ezra's time. Applying the old names to present neighbors was itself an act of interpretation, which Michael Fishbane studies as a prime example of the Bible interpreting its own laws. The law against marrying Canaanites, "Do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters for your sons" (Deuteronomy 7:3), is widened to cover all "the peoples of the lands."

a: the holy seed
p: Isaiah used the phrase for the stump left after judgment. Here it marks the people's descent as holy.
b: Isaiah 6:13 ends a vision of devastation with a stump still standing: "the holy seed is its stump." Ezra 9:2 applies the phrase to the returned community as a people set apart by descent. Earlier texts called Israel holy because God chose it (Deuteronomy 7:6) and because it keeps his commands (Leviticus 19:2). Christine Hayes argues that Ezra 9 adds a new idea, a holiness carried in the family line itself, so that marriage outside it profanes what is holy, much as a priest's choice of wife was restricted (Leviticus 21:7; Leviticus 21:14–15). Others think "seed" here simply means the people, with no theory of descent behind it. The Greek of 2 Esdras renders it literally, sperma to hagion.
orig: זֶרַע הַקֹּדֶשׁ (zera' haqqodesh), 'the seed of holiness'
r: Isaiah 6:13; Deuteronomy 7:6; Leviticus 19:2; Leviticus 21:7; Leviticus 21:14–15; Malachi 2:15

a: this unfaithfulness
p: Ma'al is the word for misusing what belongs to God. The officials treat the marriages as an offense against the holy.
b: The law uses ma'al for taking holy things into common use: "Someone may act unfaithfully and sin by mistake against the LORD's holy things" (Leviticus 5:15). Jacob Milgrom showed that the word belongs to the language of sacrilege, a wrong done to God's property. If Israel is "holy seed," mixing it with the peoples misuses something holy, and the remedy is the guilt offering of a ram, which the priests bring in 10:19. Chronicles uses the same word for the sins that caused the exile (1 Chronicles 9:1; 2 Chronicles 36:14), so the choice of word raises the stakes: this is the sin that lost the land.

a: tore out some hair from my head and my beard
t: Ezra pulls out his own hair
p: Ezra tears out his own hair in grief. Nehemiah, facing the same problem, tears at other men's (Nehemiah 13:25).
b: Tearing clothes and shaving or plucking hair were signs of mourning and horror (Job 1:20; Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 41:5). Ezra's response turns inward: he grieves as though he were the guilty one. Nehemiah later struck some of the offenders, tore at their hair and made them swear an oath (Nehemiah 13:25). The pairing is often noted: two leaders, two temperaments, one cause.

a: All who trembled at what the God of Israel had said
p: The charedim, "tremblers," took God's word with deep seriousness. Today's Haredi Jews take their name from them.
b: The same word appears in Isaiah: God looks to the one who is humble and broken in spirit and trembles at his word (Isaiah 66:2), and Isaiah 66:5 speaks to those who tremble at his word and are mocked by their own brothers. Ezra 10:3 uses it again for those who back Shecaniah's proposal. Some scholars think the "tremblers" were a recognizable group in Persian Judah, perhaps linked with the circle behind Isaiah 66. Ultra-Orthodox Jews today are called Haredim, a name drawn from these verses, for a life lived in awe of God's commands.

a: the evening grain offering
t: The hour of the evening offering
p: The daily evening offering, in the afternoon, was a set time for prayer.
b: The law prescribed a lamb and a grain offering each morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8). Elijah prayed "when the hour came for the grain offering to go up" (1 Kings 18:36), Daniel at the time of the evening offering (Daniel 9:21), and a psalm asks that lifted hands be like the evening offering (Psalm 141:2). By New Testament times the ninth hour, about 3 p.m., was the hour of prayer at the temple (Acts 3:1). Ezra sits stunned for hours, then rises to pray, kneeling with open palms as Solomon did (1 Kings 8:54), at the hour when Israel's prayers went up with the offering.
r: Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8; 1 Kings 18:36; Daniel 9:21; Psalm 141:2; Acts 3:1; 1 Kings 8:54

a: my self-humbling
p: Hebrew ta'anit means "self-humbling" or "affliction." In later Hebrew it is the ordinary word for a fast.
b: The noun comes from 'innah nefesh, "afflict oneself," the phrase the law uses for the Day of Atonement fast (Leviticus 16:29–31; Leviticus 23:27). This is its only use in the Hebrew Bible. Most versions translate it "fasting" here, and later Jewish usage made it the standard term: the Mishnah and Talmud tractate on public fasts is called Ta'anit. The Plain keeps the wider sense, since Ezra's torn clothes, pulled hair and stunned silence (9:3–4) are all part of it, not only going without food.

a: My God, I am ashamed and humiliated to lift my face toward you, my God
t: A confession that asks for nothing
p: Ezra confesses as "we," though he had not sinned in this matter, and he never asks God for anything.
b: The prayer belongs with the great confessions of the period (Nehemiah 1:5–11; Nehemiah 9:6–37; Daniel 9:4–19), all built on the pattern of Solomon's prayer for exiles who would "turn back and plead for grace" (1 Kings 8:47). Ezra begins with "I" and moves at once to "our wrongdoing." He reviews history (9:7), God's recent kindness (9:8–9) and the broken command (9:10–12), and ends by leaving the people's fate with God: "Look at us here in front of you, guilty as we are!" (9:15). There is no plea for forgiveness. Some read that as deep humility. Others hear a speech aimed at the listening crowd (10:1) as much as at God, preparing them for drastic action. Both may be true.

a: to the sword, to captivity, to looting, and to shame on our faces
p: Ezra's list matches the penalties the covenant warned of.
b: Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 warned that unfaithfulness would bring the sword, exile and plunder (Leviticus 26:33; Deuteronomy 28:36–37). Ezra reads the exile as their fulfillment and adds "just as we are now": the people are still in that state, under foreign kings. In his view the returned community lives not after judgment but inside its long shadow, a theme also of Nehemiah 9:36–37.

a: a band of survivors
p: Ezra uses two remnant words: peletah, "those who escaped," and she'erit, "what is left."
b: Both words belong to the prophets' language of hope through judgment. Isaiah promises that the escaped of the house of Judah will take root again (Isaiah 37:31–32) and names a son "A remnant will return" (Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 10:20–22). Ezra uses peletah four times (9:8, 9:13, 9:14, 9:15) and she'erit once (9:14). His fear is that the remnant could still be lost: if they sin again, God might leave "no remnant and no survivor" (9:14). The community's small size is not a failure; it is God's gift, and it is fragile.

a: a tent peg in his holy place
p: The yated was a peg driven into the ground to hold a tent. Ezra uses it for a small but firm hold.
b: Isaiah pictures Eliakim as a peg driven into a sure place, on which his whole family hangs (Isaiah 22:23), and Zechariah says the tent peg will come from Judah (Zechariah 10:4). For Ezra the peg is the rebuilt temple, or the community's foothold around it: a small thing driven in deep, so that the tent of Israel can be pitched again (Isaiah 54:2). The Greek of 2 Esdras has stērigma, "a support"; the KJV has "a nail." Some Jewish and Christian readers have seen a messianic figure in Zechariah's peg; Ezra uses the word more modestly.

a: Slaves is what we are
p: The returned community was free to worship but still subject to Persia. Ezra calls it slavery.
b: Persian rule was generous to the temple, and Ezra thanks God for the kings' kindness. Yet he will not call it freedom. Nehemiah's prayer says it more sharply: they are slaves on the very land God gave their ancestors, and its harvest goes to foreign kings (Nehemiah 9:36–37). The tension belongs to the book itself: God's loyal love reaches Israel "before the kings of Persia," through the empire rather than by ending it (see 7:28). Readers who see Ezra as a loyal servant of Persia, and those who see him as a reluctant subject, can both cite this verse.

a: a fence in Judah and Jerusalem
t: A fence or a city wall?
p: Gader is usually a wall around a vineyard or field, not a city wall. Its meaning matters for dating Ezra.
b: The word is used for the stone walls of vineyards (Numbers 22:24; Isaiah 5:5; Psalm 80:12), and "in Judah and Jerusalem" fits a protecting boundary around the whole province better than a city wall. Most commentators therefore read it as a picture of God's protection through Persian rule. Some who date Ezra after Nehemiah take it as a reference to Nehemiah's rebuilt wall (Nehemiah 6:15). The Greek of 2 Esdras has phragmos, "fence, hedge," which supports the figurative sense.

a: the commands you laid down through your servants the prophets
t: A quotation stitched from the Torah
p: Ezra cites "the prophets," but the words come from Leviticus and Deuteronomy, read together.
b: No single verse says what 9:11–12 quotes. The land defiled by its peoples comes from Leviticus 18: "For the people who lived in the land before you did all these abhorrent things, and the land became unclean" (Leviticus 18:27). The ban on marriage comes from Deuteronomy 7:3, and "never seek their peace or their good" from Deuteronomy 23:6, a law about Ammon and Moab, here made general. "From edge to edge" recalls Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with blood "brim to brim" (2 Kings 21:16). Calling Moses' words "the prophets" is not a slip: Moses was the first of the prophets (Deuteronomy 18:15; Hosea 12:13), and Ezra hears the whole Torah as God's warning through them.
r: Leviticus 18:24–30; Deuteronomy 7:1–3; Deuteronomy 23:6; 2 Kings 21:16; Deuteronomy 18:15; Hosea 12:13

a: a land of defilement
p: Niddah is the impurity of a woman's monthly flow. Ezra uses it as a picture of the land's moral defilement.
b: Leviticus uses niddah for menstrual impurity (Leviticus 15:19–24; Leviticus 18:19), which was natural and temporary. Prophets used it as a figure for sin (Ezekiel 36:17; Lamentations 1:17). Jonathan Klawans distinguishes ritual impurity, caught by contact and washed away, from moral impurity, caused by grave sins such as idolatry and sexual sin, which defiles the land itself (Leviticus 18:24–28). Ezra's language is moral: the peoples' practices defile the land. Whether he also treats the foreign women as ritually impure in themselves is debated; Christine Hayes argues the concern is the holy seed, not contagion.

a: Never seek their peace or their good, for all time
t: Deuteronomy's law about Ammon and Moab
p: Deuteronomy 23:6 says this of Ammon and Moab, who opposed Israel in the wilderness. Ezra extends it to all.
b: The law reads, "Never seek their peace or their good, all your days" (Deuteronomy 23:6). "Peace" there likely means a treaty. In Deuteronomy it explains why Ammonites and Moabites may not enter the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3–4). Ezra applies it to all the peoples of the land and to marriage, and Nehemiah 13:1–3 shows the same law read aloud and enforced. Readers have long noticed the tension with Ruth, a Moabite woman who joins Israel and becomes David's ancestor (Ruth 4:13–17). The rabbis resolved it by reading Deuteronomy's ban as applying to Moabite men only (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3).

a: have held back and not given our wrongs their full weight
p: Literally, God "held back downward, below our wrongs." He punished less than the sin deserved.
b: The phrase is unusual: chasakhta lemattah me'avonenu, "you held back to below our wrongdoing." It says that the exile, terrible as it was, fell short of the sin. Psalm 103:10 says the same thing in other words: God has not paid us back as our sins deserve. Ezra's argument follows from it: if God has held back this far, a new offense would leave no defense at all (9:14).

a: become in-laws with the peoples of these abhorrent practices
p: The verb hitchatten is the one in Deuteronomy 7:3 and in Shechem's offer to Jacob's family.
b: It means to form a marriage alliance between families. Hamor of Shechem proposed it to Jacob's sons (Genesis 34:9), Deuteronomy forbade it with Canaan's nations (Deuteronomy 7:3), and Joshua warned against it (Joshua 23:12). Solomon formed such an alliance with Pharaoh (1 Kings 3:1). The word shows that the issue was not only private love but alliances between families, with land, property and religion bound up in them.

a: you are in the right
p: Tsaddiq can mean God is just in punishing, or righteous in saving. Ezra may mean both.
b: Confessions often declare God in the right and the people guilty (Nehemiah 9:33; Daniel 9:7; Lamentations 1:18). Ezra adds "We have been left as a band of survivors," which suggests a second sense: God's righteousness shows in keeping a remnant alive, as in Isaiah and the Psalms, where righteousness and saving go together (Isaiah 45:21; Psalm 71:15). He ends without asking for anything; the verdict is in God's hands.

a: Ezra was praying and making confession
p: Ezra's "I" gives way to a narrator who speaks of "Ezra." The memoir may be retold from here on.
b: Chapter 10 reads like a report by someone else, perhaps the book's editor working from Ezra's memoir. It shows what Ezra's private grief had set in motion: a crowd of men, women and children weeping with him. Ezra had thrown himself down in front of the temple, where people could see him; whether or not he meant it as a sign, it worked as one. 1 Esdras 8–9 tells the same events, often in different words, and then goes straight on to Ezra's reading of the law.

a: Shecaniah son of Jehiel, of the descendants of Elam
t: A man with family at stake
p: A Jehiel of the clan of Elam is among the men listed in 10:26. Shecaniah may be speaking against his own father.
b: If the Jehiel of 10:26 is Shecaniah's father, then the proposal to send away the wives cost his own family, perhaps his own mother. That is possible, though Jehiel was a common name. Shecaniah speaks for the guilty as "we," as Ezra did, and his words give Ezra what the prayer had not asked for: a way forward. (The written Hebrew spells the clan Olam here; the margin reads Elam, as in 2:7 and 8:7.)

a: We have taken foreign wives into our homes
p: The text never names their peoples or says they worshiped other gods. Readers identify them in different ways.
b: The verb is unusual: hoshiv, "settle, give a home to," used for marriage only in Ezra–Nehemiah (10:2, 10:10, 10:14, 10:17–18; Nehemiah 13:23, 13:27). Who were the women? (1) Foreigners from the neighboring peoples, like the Ashdodite, Ammonite and Moabite wives of Nehemiah 13:23, whose children could not speak the language of Judah. (2) Judeans and Israelites who had never gone into exile, now counted among "the peoples of the land" by the returnees; Daniel Smith-Christopher and Tamara Eskenazi with Eleanore Judd argue this, and on their view the dispute was also about land, inheritance and status. (3) A mix of both, in a province where the lines between groups were blurred. The text's own reason is religious: such marriages had turned Israel to other gods before (9:1; Deuteronomy 7:4).

a: there is hope for Israel over this
p: Miqveh, "hope," is a rare word. Shecaniah turns despair into a plan.
b: The same word appears in Jeremiah, where God is "the hope of Israel" (Jeremiah 14:8; Jeremiah 17:13), and in David's prayer that life on earth is like a shadow with no hope (1 Chronicles 29:15). Ezra's prayer had ended without a request; Shecaniah's "there is hope" opens the way to action. Rabbi Akiva played on a second meaning of miqveh, a pool for ritual washing: as a pool makes the unclean clean, so God makes Israel clean (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

a: to send out all the wives and the children born of them
p: The plan includes the children. The text records no word from the women and nothing of what became of them.
b: The verb is hotsi', "send out," not the divorce word shillach, and no certificate is mentioned (Deuteronomy 24:1). The children presumably went with their mothers. Saving a fragile community: Kidner and Williamson see a small group facing absorption and the loss of its faith, taking a terrible step to survive. Exclusion at the cost of the weakest: Harold Washington, David Janzen and Willa Johnson read the reform as the returnees' elite drawing a boundary, and Katherine Southwood as the making of an ethnic identity. Their case at its strongest: no law of Moses commands divorce; Deuteronomy 23:7–8 admits Egyptians after three generations, yet 9:1 bans them; the text never says these women worshiped other gods; Isaiah 56:3 uses the same verb, badal, to promise the foreigner who joins the LORD that he will not be separated from his people; and children are put out for their parents' marriages. A legal reading: later rabbinic law held that such a marriage had no legal force, so no divorce was needed, and that a child follows the mother's status (Bavli Kiddushin 68b); Shaye Cohen argues that this rule is later than Ezra.
orig: לְהוֹצִיא כָל־נָשִׁים וְהַנּוֹלָד מֵהֶם (lehotsi' khol-nashim vehannolad mehem)
r: Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Deuteronomy 23:7–8; Isaiah 56:3; Deuteronomy 7:3–4; 10:44; Nehemiah 13:23–27; Malachi 2:14–16

a: Let it be done by the law
p: No law of Moses commands sending away foreign wives. Shecaniah applies the laws against making such marriages.
b: Deuteronomy 7:3 forbids marrying the nations of Canaan, and Deuteronomy 24:1–4 regulates divorce, but neither tells a man to send away a wife he already has. The nearest precedents are Abraham sending away Hagar and Ishmael (Genesis 21:10–14) and the law of the captive wife (Deuteronomy 21:14). Shecaniah reasons that a marriage the law forbade should be undone, a step of interpretation rather than a quotation. Malachi, perhaps from the same period, condemns both marrying "the daughter of a foreign god" (Malachi 2:11) and breaking faith with the wife of one's youth (Malachi 2:14–16), holding the two concerns side by side.

a: Be strong and get it done
p: The same pair of verbs David used to charge Solomon to build the temple.
b: Chazaq va'aseh, "be strong and act," is David's charge to Solomon: "Be strong, and get it done" (1 Chronicles 28:10; compare 1 Chronicles 28:20). Shecaniah gives Ezra the same charge for a different kind of building: rebuilding the community's holiness. Like Joshua's commission (Joshua 1:6–9), the words fall on a leader about to do something hard.

a: the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib
p: A Jehohanan son of Eliashib was high priest around 410 BC. If he is meant, Ezra came after Nehemiah.
b: Eliashib was high priest in Nehemiah's day (Nehemiah 3:1; Nehemiah 13:28), and Nehemiah 12:22–23 names a Johanan "son of Eliashib" among the later high priests. An Aramaic letter from Elephantine, dated 407 BC, mentions "Johanan the high priest" in Jerusalem. Those who date Ezra to 398 BC (Artaxerxes II) see here the room of a high priest's family in his time. Those who keep 458 BC answer that Jehohanan and Eliashib were common names, that the room may be called by the name of a later owner, or that this Jehohanan was a young man, not yet high priest, in 458. See the chapter page on the dating.

a: he did not eat food or drink water
p: Going without both food and water recalls Moses' fast after the golden calf.
b: Moses says, "Bread I did not eat, and water I did not drink, because of all the sin you had committed" (Deuteronomy 9:18). A fast without water was rare and extreme (Esther 4:16; Jonah 3:7). Ezra, like Moses, grieves over the people's sin as an intercessor, not as one of the guilty. Jewish tradition's picture of Ezra as a second Moses (Bavli Sanhedrin 21b) draws on scenes like this.

a: would have all his goods put under the ban
p: Yocharam is the verb of cherem: property "devoted" to God. The rabbis built a principle of law on this verse.
b: Under the ban, property was taken from its owner and given to the sanctuary or destroyed (Leviticus 27:28; Joshua 6:17–19). Here the threat is loss of goods to the temple and exclusion from the community, a forerunner of later Jewish excommunication, also called cherem. The Talmud derives from this verse the rule that property a court declares ownerless is ownerless: a court's power to transfer property for the public good (Bavli Yevamot 89b; Bavli Gittin 36b). The Greek of 2 Esdras has anathematisthēsetai, "will be put under a curse," from the word that gives English "anathema."

a: It was the twentieth day of the ninth month
p: The ninth month, Kislev, falls in November–December, the heart of the rainy season.
b: In 458 BC the date would fall in December. Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet up, and its winter rain is cold. The people sitting in the temple court were "shaking over the matter and from the downpours," a detail with the feel of an eyewitness, and the plea of 10:13 follows naturally. In the same month a king of Judah once sat in his winter house with a fire burning (Jeremiah 36:22). The hearings ran from the first of the tenth month to the first of the first month (10:16–17), right through the winter.

a: make your confession to the LORD
p: Todah means both "thanks, praise" and "confession." To confess sin is to give God his due.
b: Joshua told Achan to "give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make your confession to him" (Joshua 7:19). Confessing wrong admits that God is right (9:15), which is a kind of praise. The Greek of 2 Esdras chose "praise" (ainesis); 1 Esdras 9:8 has both, "confession, glory." The Plain follows the sense the context needs.

a: Set yourselves apart from the peoples of the land
p: Badal, "separate," is a verb of creation and of holiness, and a key word in Ezra–Nehemiah.
b: God separated light from darkness (Genesis 1:4) and Israel from the peoples: "I have set you apart from the peoples to be mine" (Leviticus 20:26). Ezra–Nehemiah uses the verb at its turning points: those who had separated from the nations' uncleanness kept the Passover (6:21), the officials complain that the people have not separated (9:1), the people now separate (10:11, 10:16), and later they separate from all foreigners (Nehemiah 9:2; Nehemiah 10:28; Nehemiah 13:3). Notice 6:21: outsiders who separated themselves from the nations' ways could join Israel. On that verse at least, the separation is from practices, and the door is not wholly shut.

a: took a stand against this
p: The Hebrew 'amedu 'al zot can mean "stood against this" or "stood over this," that is, took charge of it.
b: Most modern translations read opposition: four men objected, perhaps finding the plan too harsh, or the delay too soft. The KJV reads "were employed about this matter," and 1 Esdras 9:14 says they "took it on," making them its managers; the Greek of 2 Esdras has "were with me in this" (see the variant). If they opposed it, Meshullam may be the Meshullam who had a foreign wife (10:29). If they managed it, they are the officials of 10:14. The grammar slightly favors opposition, since 'amad 'al often means to rise against (Daniel 8:25; 1 Chronicles 21:1).

a: From the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers
p: The list starts at the top, with the family of Jeshua, the high priest who rebuilt the altar (3:2).
b: Members of the high priestly family had married outside Israel, as Nehemiah later found with Eliashib's grandson, who was Sanballat's son-in-law (Nehemiah 13:28). The rabbis linked this verse with Zechariah's vision of Joshua the high priest in filthy clothes (Zechariah 3:3–4): the stains, they said, were that his sons married women not fit for the priesthood (Bavli Sanhedrin 93a). The priests alone pledge with a handshake and bring a guilt ram (10:19), perhaps because more was expected of them (Leviticus 21:7; Leviticus 21:14). The Hebrew names the father Jozadak here; Chronicles has the fuller form Jehozadak.
r: 3:2; Zechariah 3:1–5; Nehemiah 13:28; Haggai 1:1; Leviticus 21:7; Leviticus 21:14; 1 Chronicles 6:14–15

a: they brought a ram from the flock for their guilt
p: The ram is the guilt offering the law requires for ma'al, unfaithfulness against holy things.
b: Leviticus 5:15 prescribes "a flawless ram from the flock" as the guilt offering of one who acts unfaithfully against the LORD's holy things. The officials had called the marriages ma'al (9:2), and the priests now pay the price the law sets for sacrilege. The Hebrew is compressed ("and guilty, a ram of the flock for their guilt"). Some scholars read ashamam, "their guilt offering," for ashemim, "guilty," a difference of one letter. "They gave their hand" is a pledge sealed by a handshake (2 Kings 10:15; 1 Chronicles 29:24).

a: And of Israel
p: The list names 17 priests; 10 Levites, singers and gatekeepers; and 86 laymen: 113 men in the Hebrew.
b: If 10:38 is read with the Greek as "of the descendants of Binnui" rather than as two more names, the total is 111. Either way it is a small number beside the thousands of the community (2:64; 8:1–14). That suggests either that the problem touched only some families, or that the list records only the leading cases. The order (priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, then lay Israel) runs from the holiest down, the reverse of chapter 2, which began with the lay families. Many of the clan names repeat those of the first return (2:3–20).

a: Some of them had wives by whom they had had children.
p: The book ends with a sentence that seems broken. Translators read it, and its outcome, in different ways.
b: The Hebrew says literally, "and there were among them women, and they placed sons." The verb "placed" (vayyasimu) is masculine and strange for having children. Readings: (1) the Plain's, close to the KJV: some of the men had children by these wives; (2) with a small change to the verb, "some of the wives had borne children"; (3) 1 Esdras 9:36, "and they sent them away with their children," which the RSV and NRSV follow; the BHS apparatus and Wilhelm Rudolph reconstruct a Hebrew text behind it, roughly "and they sent them away, wives and children," so this is more than a paraphrase; (4) the Greek of 2 Esdras, "and they had fathered sons from them." Only (3) says the sending away happened. As the Hebrew stands, the book ends with the list and the children, not with a report that the men obeyed. Nehemiah 13:23–27 shows the issue rising again a generation later.
orig: וְיֵשׁ מֵהֶם נָשִׁים וַיָּשִׂימוּ בָּנִים (veyesh mehem nashim vayyasimu banim)
